sourceContext: US UI/UX design agency; this industry page serves B2B and enterprise software companies that need admin, permission and data-heavy platform design.
abstract: SaaS UI UX design shapes the user interface (UI) and user experience (UX) of business software sold as a service, from multi-tenant admin consoles to single sign-on (SSO) and data-heavy tables. Our software-as-a-service (SaaS) platform engagements run 8–16 weeks, cost $60,000–$180,000, and end with enterprise-ready workflows and a design system.

sections.h2: What is SaaS UI UX design?
sections.answer: SaaS UI UX design is the design of business software sold on subscription, covering the admin console, role-based access control, SSO and the data tables that customer teams use every day. The work serves 2 audiences at once: end users inside a customer account and the IT administrators who buy, configure and audit the product.
sections.body: Every tenant holds its own users, roles, integrations and contract terms, so each screen separates account-level settings from personal settings. Lifecycle work on trials, activation and churn belongs to our SaaS UX design engagement; this page covers the platform layer that enterprise deals depend on.

sections.h2: Which parts of a B2B SaaS platform do we design?
sections.answer: We design 6 types of B2B SaaS products: multi-tenant admin consoles, role and permission managers, SSO and provisioning setup, data-heavy tables, integration settings and audit logs.

items.title: Multi-tenant admin consoles.
items.body: Workspace owners manage users and licences per tenant, for example a seat-allocation screen.

items.title: Role and permission managers.
items.body: Administrators define who reads, edits or approves each object, for example a permission matrix comparing 4 roles across 20 resources.

items.title: SSO and provisioning setup.
items.body: IT teams connect an identity provider such as Okta or Microsoft Entra ID, for example a guided Security Assertion Markup Language (SAML) setup with a test-connection step.

items.title: Data-heavy tables and reporting.
items.body: Analysts filter and export thousands of records, for example saved views and bulk actions in a 10,000-row table.

items.title: Integration and developer settings.
items.body: Technical admins manage API keys and webhooks, for example a key-rotation flow showing the last-used date.

items.title: Audit logs and compliance centres.
items.body: Security reviewers trace every change, for example an event log with actor, IP address and before-and-after values.

sections.h2: What UX challenges are specific to SaaS?
sections.answer: 4 UX challenges are specific to SaaS: the split between buyer and user, permission complexity, tenant-specific configuration and data density on shared screens.

items.title: Buyer and user split
items.body: The IT director who signs the contract never runs the daily workflow, so research covers administrators, end users and security reviewers separately.

items.title: Permission complexity
items.body: Custom roles, field-level permissions and approval chains multiply the states each screen must show, for example a read-only version of an editable form.

items.title: Tenant-specific configuration
items.body: Two customers on the same release see different menus and fields, so designers specify every screen with custom fields, hidden modules and white-labelled branding.

items.title: Data density on shared screens
items.body: Power users want 50 columns and keyboard shortcuts while occasional users want 5 clear columns, so tables need saved views and density settings.

sections.h2: How does our SaaS UI UX design process work?
sections.answer: Our B2B platform design process takes 8–16 weeks (40–80 working days) and runs in 5 steps, from the role and tenant audit to the design system handover.

items.title: Role and tenant audit (5–10 days)
items.body: We list every role, permission and tenant setting and interview administrators, end users and a customer security reviewer.

items.title: Permission and object modelling (5–10 days)
items.body: Designers map which role sees, edits and approves each object in a permission matrix that product, engineering and sales sign off.

items.title: Admin and workflow design (15–30 days)
items.body: Designers produce the admin console, SSO setup, tables and audit log in Figma, with empty, read-only, error and over-limit states.

items.title: Enterprise readiness review (5–10 days)
items.body: 5 administrators per round test the prototype, and a Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.2 AA check keeps the Accessibility Conformance Report (ACR) consistent with the interface.

items.title: Design system handover (10–20 days)
items.body: Developers receive documented Figma components for tables, filters and permission editors.

sections.h2: Enterprise SaaS UX vs consumer app UX
sections.answer: SaaS UX designs for many roles inside many customer accounts; general product UX designs for 1 user group completing its own tasks. Enterprise procurement and tenant settings add work a consumer product never needs.

sections.h2: How much does SaaS UI UX design cost?
sections.answer: Full SaaS platform design costs $60,000–$180,000 and takes 8–16 weeks, including a design system. The price depends on 4 factors: the number of roles, tenant configuration options, data-heavy tables and enterprise readiness features such as SSO.
sections.body: An admin console redesign with 3 roles fits a $25,000–$60,000 sprint over 4–8 weeks. A full platform with 8 roles, custom fields, SSO and a component library for 3 product teams sits near $180,000. Teams that need finance sign-off for the component library can model when a shared component library pays back before they request a quote.

sections.h2: Which security and procurement standards shape SaaS UX?
sections.answer: 5 standards and regulations shape SaaS UX:
items: SOC 2: auditors check access controls, so admin screens need access reviews, session timeouts and an exportable audit log.
SAML 2.0 and System for Cross-domain Identity Management (SCIM): SSO and automatic provisioning need setup screens and clear mapping errors.
WCAG 2.2 level AA: dense tables and modals need keyboard access, visible focus and 4.5:1 text contrast.
Section 508 and the VPAT: US federal buyers request an ACR, so every claim must match the shipped interface.
General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) and California Consumer Privacy Act (CCPA): tenant admins need data export, user deletion and retention settings.

sections.answer: These answers cover the 5 questions B2B software teams ask most about SaaS platform design.

faqs.q: Do you design admin consoles for multi-tenant SaaS?
faqs.a: Yes. Admin console design covers users, roles, licences, billing and audit logs per tenant, with separate screens for customer workspace owners and the vendor's support team.

faqs.q: Does SaaS platform design include SSO setup screens?
faqs.a: Yes. SSO setup design covers the identity provider choice, SAML 2.0 or OpenID Connect fields, a test-connection step and error messages that tell an IT administrator which attribute mapping failed.

faqs.q: What kind of document is a permission matrix?
faqs.a: A permission matrix is both. Designers draft roles, objects and actions, and engineering builds access rules from the same matrix, so interface and back end match.

faqs.q: Can enterprise data tables stay usable with 50 or more columns?
faqs.a: Yes. Saved views, column pinning and per-role column presets keep wide tables usable, if each user group gets its own default view instead of 1 shared layout. When those tables are redesigned, carrying admins' saved views through the migration keeps whole accounts from churning.

faqs.q: How long does SaaS platform design take?
faqs.a: Full SaaS platform design takes 8–16 weeks, which equals 40–80 working days. A single admin console or permission redesign takes 4–8 weeks as a research and design sprint.
